title: Webhook Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Webhook Security.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Webhook Security and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Webhook Security, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 15: API, GraphQL, WebSocket, and Webhook Security. It builds practical understanding of Webhook Security with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Webhook Security addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Webhook Security can be understood through this sequence: Define operation → Authenticate request → Authorize object + field → Bound load + audit. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 113.1 Inbound and outbound webhook architecture; 113.2 Message authenticity and signature verification; 113.3 Timestamp and replay protections; 113.4 Event ordering and duplicate delivery; 113.5 Safe outbound URL configuration; 113.6 Retry policies and secret rotation. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Pseudocode: provider verification and storage APIs are placeholders. Verify the provider’s exact signature scheme and implement the processed-event write atomically with the business side effect.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Webhook Security”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Webhook Security in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Webhook Security is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
